mapper.verbatim_quote:
the police officer or authorised person may —
(a) issue a written order to require a person in whose possession or power the document or thing is believed to be —
(i) to produce the document or thing at the time and place stated in the order
mapper.rationale: Police/authorised persons can compel production of or access to documents/data (including personal data) without any court order or independent judicial authorization; qualifies as government access without judicial oversight.

verifier.reason: SG CPC 2010 s.20(1) permits police officers of sergeant rank or above (and authorised persons) to issue written orders requiring production of documents/things or access to them—including electronic/digital data—without requiring a court order or independent judicial authorization. The provision explicitly states the police officer "considers" necessity; there is no requirement for a judicial warrant, court order, or approval by an independent tribunal. This enables government access to personal data without the explicit authorization of an independent judicial body, directly triggering 7.5's scoring branch (1). The trap checks confirm: (a) this IS an access provision beyond privacy law (in the CPC); (b) judicial oversight is absent—a police/authorised-person determination suffices; (c) 7.5 applies to personal data access by government without independent judicial authorization. The provision unambiguously permits such access.

mapper.verbatim_quote: An organisation must designate one or more individuals to be responsible for ensuring that the organisation complies with this Act.
mapper.rationale: Mandatory DPO-equivalent designation requirement applying to all organisations under the horizontal PDPA -> DPO requirement across all sectors.

verifier.reason: SG PDPA 2012 s.11(3) requires an organisation to designate one or more individuals responsible for ensuring compliance with the Act. This is a DATA PROTECTION OFFICER (DPO) requirement — the designated individual(s) bear responsibility for personal-data-protection compliance. The Act applies horizontally across all sectors (PDPA 2012 is Singapore's comprehensive data-protection law). However, s.11(3) does NOT mandate a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) separately; it is a DPO-only requirement. Per the TRAP rule (Guide p.61): "The duty must be MANDATORY. Advisory/recommended DPIAs...do not create a DPIA mandate — Singapore scores on its mandatory DPO duty." Since the DPO requirement applies to ALL sectors (horizontal scope), the scoring tree fires on the first branch: "A DPO requirement applies to ALL sectors" → score 1. But the provision text provided is incomplete (cut off at "must make available to the public the busine[ss]"), so I apply a confidence penalty. The controlling law (PDPA 2012 as a comprehensive framework) confirms horizontal applicability, scoring 1 under the DPO-all-sectors branch.

escalation.reason: s.11(3) mandates every organisation designate individual(s) responsible for PDPA compliance — this is the DPO requirement under 7.4. It is horizontal (applies to all organisations/sectors, not sector-specific), and mandatory ("must designate"), not advisory. Fires branch 1. Not a mere compliance/security officer trap: the role is responsibility for data-protection compliance.

mapper.verbatim_quote: An organisation must not transfer any personal data to a country or territory outside Singapore except in accordance with requirements prescribed under this Act to ensure that organisations provide a standard of protection to personal data so transferred that is comparable to the protection under this Act.
mapper.rationale: Default-prohibition-with-exception pattern covering personal data horizontally = conditional flow regime scoring 1 regardless of sector.

verifier.reason: Section 26(1) PDPA 2012 establishes a conditional flow regime: transfer of personal data outside Singapore is prohibited by default ("must not transfer") UNLESS conditions are met ("except in accordance with requirements prescribed under this Act to ensure...comparable...protection"). This satisfies the 6.4 definition: conditions businesses must satisfy to transfer data across borders. The trap check confirms this is NOT 6.1 (no absolute ban—a compliant transfer path exists via prescribed requirements). The provision covers PERSONAL DATA (defined in Act as information relating to identified/identifiable individuals), triggering the first branch of the 6.4 scoring tree: "The conditional regime covers PERSONAL data — regardless of whether it is horizontal or sector-specific" → score 1.

mapper.verbatim_quote: The purpose of this Act is to govern the collection, use and disclosure of personal data by organisations in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need of organisations to collect, use or disclose personal data for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances.
mapper.rationale: PDPA 2012 is a comprehensive horizontal data-protection law covering organisations generally; economy-level framework exists -> lack-indicator scores 0.

Section 3 (Purpose) and s.4 (Application) cite the PDPA 2012's scope and application, but individual provisions are not separate 7.1 discoveries. The economy-level answer is: Singapore HAS a comprehensive DP framework (PDPA 2012 applies horizontally). Score 0 once per SG, not per provision.

escalation.reason: SG PDPA 2012 is the comprehensive, horizontal data-protection framework; its purpose/application provisions (ss.3-4) evidence a cross-sectoral law governing collection, use and disclosure of personal data by organisations. Inverted polarity: existence of a comprehensive framework → 0. Economy-level answer cited via scope provision.

mapper.verbatim_quote: The company must retain the records referred to in subsection (1) for a period of not less than 5 years from the end of the financial year in which the transactions or operations to which those records relate are completed.
mapper.rationale: Explicit minimum retention period (not less than 5 years) for corporate accounting records satisfies 7.3 minimum-retention branch.

verifier.reason: Section 199(2) of the Singapore Companies Act 1967 imposes a mandatory minimum period retention requirement: companies "must retain the records...for a period of not less than 5 years from the end of the financial year." This explicitly states a minimum duration (5 years) using the mandated language "not less than." The trap checks confirm applicability: (1) this is a MINIMUM-period rule (specified floor: "not less than 5"), not a maximum-period "as long as necessary" rule; (2) the duration is clearly specified (5 years), not a prescribed period without a number; (3) the measure applies to commercial transaction records, within scope for 7.3. The trap distinguishing retention (DURATION) from storage (LOCATION) is satisfied—this is about how long, not where. The scoring tree fires on the first branch: "A requirement exists to retain data for at least a specified minimum period (duration in days/months/years explicitly stated...)" → score 1.

mapper.verbatim_quote:
there must be sent to and kept at a place in
Singapore and be at all times open to inspection by the directors such statements and returns with respect to the business dealt with in the records so kept
mapper.rationale: Requires copy of accounting statements/returns be kept in Singapore even if records kept abroad; sector-specific (corporate accounting records), so category (2) -> 0.5.

verifier.reason: Section 199(4) is a record-keeping rule for corporate accounting documents, not a data localization measure. It mandates that accounting records kept outside Singapore be accompanied by summaries kept in Singapore for inspection by directors—a general corporate governance requirement, not a DATA STORAGE requirement as defined in 6.2. The provision governs WHERE BOOKS/RECORDS are kept for audit purposes, not the localization of personal data processing. The TRAP in 6.2 disambiguation explicitly states: "A duty to keep books or records, with no requirement about where they are kept, is not 6.2" (Indicator Reference row 83). Conversely, this requires copies in Singapore, but for financial audit compliance, not data localization tied to cross-border transfer restrictions. The commercial-data-localization indicators (6.1–6.4) target measures affecting data flows in commercial transactions; corporate accounting retention for audit purposes falls outside that scope.

escalation.reason: s.199(4) requires that where accounting records are kept outside SG, statements/returns be sent to and kept at a place IN Singapore — a domestic-copy storage locus (LOCATION), while records may still reside abroad. This is a 6.2 local-storage requirement, not mere general record-keeping (Ref row 83 trap cleared: it specifies in-country residence). Sectoral/specific data type (accounting data) → category (2) → 0.5. Not 7.3 (no duration), not 6.3 (no build mandate).
